youtube_description:
🔋 From $1,000/kWh to near-$100/kWh—this is the battery crash that rewired the EV industry.

In this chart-race, we visualize how the global lithium-ion EV pack cost curve collapsed, while demand powerhouses (Tesla and BYD) scaled fast—and incentive dependence eased as sticker prices improved.

⏱️ Chapters
00:00 — The starting point: EV batteries still expensive
01:40 — 2014–2017: accelerating learning curves
03:15 — 2018–2019: the “almost there” surge
05:00 — 2020–2021: cost stabilization, supply shifts
06:30 — 2022: the spike that scared the market
08:10 — 2023–2025: recovery and steep affordability gains
10:00 — Who benefits most when prices fall?

📌 What to watch
• Pack cost trajectory vs. storage demand growth
• How a temporary 2022 price shock changes the pace
• Why demand leaders still win as costs trend down

instagram_caption:
🚨 The $1,000/kWh Battery Boom just turned into a price collapse—watch who won.

In 2010, the EV world was still paying the “early-era tax.” The global lithium‑ion EV pack cost sat around **$1,000/kWh**, basically making mass EV adoption feel like a distant future dream. Then reality hit: every factory line learned faster, yields improved, and economies of scale started biting.

From **2012 to 2017**, costs fell hard—from about **$650/kWh** down to roughly **$230/kWh**. That’s not a gentle decline; it’s the kind of trend that flips spreadsheets overnight. As the cost curve dropped, demand followed like a fuse catching. Tesla’s storage demand climbed from **~5 GWh (2012)** to **~60 GWh (2017)**, while BYD accelerated even more aggressively—from **~2 GWh** to **~55 GWh** in the same window.

Then came the dramatic mid-course of the race. By **2018–2019**, pack costs were approaching the “affordability era” (about **$175/kWh in 2018** to **$137/kWh in 2019**). Tesla’s demand kept expanding (**~85 → 95 GWh**), and BYD pushed even harder (**~85 → 110 GWh**). But markets are never linear—2022 landed a punch: pack costs jumped to about **$151/kWh**, the kind of shock that can make investors panic and planners scramble.

Here’s the plot twist: leaders didn’t stall permanently. Demand kept compounding. BYD climbed from **~320 GWh (2022)** to **~470 GWh (2025E)**, while Tesla moved from **~225 GWh** to **~295 GWh**. At the same time, incentive dependence in North America fell from around **55% (2010)** to about **31% (2025E)**—meaning cheaper batteries increasingly meant less “subsidy math” holding the market together.

📉 So the question: when battery prices swing, do you think the next winners will be the companies with the cheapest manufacturing—or the ones with the fastest scaling demand?

facebook_caption:
The “EV Battery Price Crash” is one of the defining economic shifts of the last decade. Global lithium‑ion EV pack costs declined from about **$1,000/kWh (2010)** to around **$137/kWh (2019)**, driven by learning curves, scaling, and manufacturing improvements.

However, the trend didn’t stay smooth. In **2022**, pack costs spiked back to approximately **$151/kWh**, reflecting supply-chain stress and commodity/input volatility. Even with that shock, the industry’s demand engines—especially major storage consumers—continued scaling: Tesla’s energy storage demand rose from **~120 GWh (2020)** to **~295 GWh (2025E)**, while BYD grew even faster from **~140 GWh (2020)** to **~470 GWh (2025E)**.

A key signal of affordability is how policy support changes as prices fall. A proxy “incentive dependence index” for North America declines from roughly **55% (2010)** to about **31% (2025E)**, indicating that lower battery costs increasingly improved EV economics without relying as heavily on incentives.

Bottom line: when the cost curve drops, the market rewards the companies that can scale demand through volatility.

threads_caption:
Okay, THIS is the chart that explains why EVs stopped feeling like “someday” and started feeling like “now.” 🔋

In 2010, battery packs were about **$1,000/kWh**. By 2019, they were near **$137/kWh**—that’s a massive affordability jump. Then 2022 hit with a shock and costs bounced to around **$151/kWh**… and everybody thought the slowdown would stick.

But the winners didn’t freeze. Tesla demand went from **~120 GWh (2020)** to **~295 GWh (2025E)**, and BYD went from **~140 GWh** to **~470 GWh**. Meanwhile, incentive dependence in North America drops from ~**55%** to ~**31%** as battery costs fall.

So here’s the real question: if prices swing again, who do you think wins first—manufacturers with the lowest costs, or the companies with the fastest demand scaling?
